label: Pleomorphic_Adenoma
answer_markdown:
## Key Facts

- Most common salivary gland neoplasm; majority arise in parotid (~84%), but may be seen in submandibular/minor glands  
- Biphasic/“triphasic” tumor: ductal epithelial and myoepithelial cells in variable stroma (myxoid, chondroid, hyaline, fibrous)  
- Well-circumscribed/encapsulated in major glands; circumscribed (not usually encapsulated) in minor glands  
- Recurrence risk tied to incomplete excision and capsular pseudopods; malignant transformation risk is ~5% (risk increases with multiple recurrences, submandibular location, older age, larger size, prominent hyalinization, increased mitotic rate, and radiation exposure)  
- PLAG1 or HMGA2 gene rearrangements occur in ~70%—these are often mutually exclusive, but sometimes overlap ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandspleomorphicadenoma.html))  

## Terminology

- Definition: Benign salivary gland neoplasm with epithelial, myoepithelial, and variable mesenchymal-like stroma  
- Synonyms: Benign mixed tumor, mixed tumor  
- ICD-O: 8940/0 (“pleomorphic adenoma”)  
- “Mixed tumor” is synonymous; “benign mixed tumor” is less current  
- Overlaps with “myoepithelioma” if minimal ductal/cartilaginous differentiation is present ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandspleomorphicadenoma.html))  
- “Congenital pleomorphic adenoma” is not recommended terminology; true congenital variants are classified as salivary gland anlage tumor (SGAT, a hamartomatous lesion distinct from PA) ([WHO](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/WHO/WHO_HTML/HN/Salivary_Gland_Anlage_Tumour.html), [Hn Gnepp, p.448](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/HN_Gnepp.pdf#page=448))  

## Essential and Desirable Diagnostic Criteria

- **Essential:**  
  - Well-circumscribed or encapsulated mass (major glands thick capsule; minor glands usually circumscribed, lacking a true capsule)  
  - Triphasic (“biphasic”) architecture:  
    - Ductal epithelial cells forming inner layer of glands/tubules  
    - Myoepithelial cells as outer layer of cysts/tubules and scattered in stroma (plasmacytoid, spindle, clear, epithelioid, stellate morphologies)  
    - Extracellular stroma (myxoid, chondroid, hyaline, fibrous components)  
  - Absence of features of malignancy: no frank invasion, necrosis, or marked cytologic atypia  
  - PLAG1 (8q12) or HMGA2 (12q14-15) gene rearrangements are present in the majority (~70%) ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandspleomorphicadenoma.html))  
- **Desirable:**  
  - Stromal metaplasia (osseous, squamous, sebaceous, adipose, mucinous)  
  - Nuclear positivity by IHC for PLAG1 or HMGA2 (surrogate for the corresponding gene fusion, if performed)  
  - Chondroid or myxochondroid matrix  
  - Tyrosine crystals and/or intravascular tumor emboli (the latter does not correlate with recurrence or metastasis if otherwise typical)  

## Etiology/Pathogenesis

- PLAG1 fusion (~70% of cases, chromosome 8q12) or HMGA2 fusion (~70% of cases, chromosome 12q14-15); these are often mutually exclusive, but can overlap ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandspleomorphicadenoma.html))  
- Prior radiation is a risk factor for development ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandspleomorphicadenoma.html))  
- Origin thought to be from ductal reserve or myoepithelial cells  
- Salivary gland anlage tumor (SGAT) is a distinct congenital hamartomatous lesion, not a true pleomorphic adenoma ([WHO](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/WHO/WHO_HTML/HN/Salivary_Gland_Anlage_Tumour.html))  

## Clinical Issues

  - **Epidemiology:**  
    - Most common salivary gland tumor in children and adults ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandspleomorphicadenoma.html)), [Hn Thompson, p.294](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/HN_Thompson.pdf#page=294)  
    - ~54–76% of all salivary neoplasms  
    - Wide age range, peak 4th–6th decade, slight female predominance  
  - **Sites:**  
    - Parotid (most common, ~84%), submandibular, sublingual, minor glands—the palate is especially common for minor gland tumor  
  - **Presentation:**  
    - Slow-growing, painless, well-circumscribed/mobile mass  
    - Tumors can be present for years prior to excision  
  - **Natural History & Prognosis:**  
    - Recurrences are most often due to incomplete excision (esp. in parotid due to pseudopods/tongue-like extensions)—recurrences typically occur within 18 months but can present up to 50 years later ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandspleomorphicadenoma.html))  
    - Malignant transformation risk is ~5%, and is increased with multiple recurrences, submandibular site, older age, larger tumors, prominent hyalinization, increased mitotic rate, and prior radiation ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandspleomorphicadenoma.html))  
  - **Treatment:**  
    - Complete surgical resection with negative margin is curative  
    - Enucleation alone is not recommended (recurrence risk 15–25%)  
    - Radiation therapy reserved for unresectable or recurrent cases  

## Macroscopic

- Well-circumscribed, encapsulated (major glands) or circumscribed (minor glands) mass  
- Cut surface: tan-white, firm, lobulated or bosselated, with myxoid and/or cartilaginous areas ([Hn Gnepp, p.472](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/HN_Gnepp.pdf#page=472), [Hn Atlas, p.978](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/HN_Atlas.pdf#page=978))  
![Encapsulated, bosselated parotid pleomorphic adenoma](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/imgau/salivaryglandspleomorphicadenomagross01.jpg)
- Size: 1–6 cm (may be larger)  
- Recurrent tumors characteristically show multiple, variably sized nodules (“shotgun pellet-like”), especially in the parotid after prior excision ([Hn Thompson, p.297](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/HN_Thompson.pdf#page=297))  
![Shotgun pellet-like recurrent tumor](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/imgau/salivaryglandspleomorphicadenomaxu03new.jpg)
- Pseudopods/tongue-like protrusions beyond capsule may be seen, especially in parotid  
- Often solid, may have gelatinous/myxoid/translucent and cartilaginous regions  

## Microscopic

- Encapsulated or at least circumscribed, often with pseudopodic extension into adjacent tissue/fat ([Hn Atlas, p.979](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/HN_Atlas.pdf#page=979))  
- Triphasic composition:
  - Glands/tubules: ductal epithelial cells, sometimes with luminal PAS+ secretions  
  - Myoepithelial cells (plasmacytoid, spindle, epithelioid, clear, stellate); surround ducts and scatter in stroma  
  - Stroma: myxoid, chondroid, myxochondroid, hyaline, or fibrous; stroma-rich variants may recur more
  - Metaplasia observed—osseous, sebaceous, adipose, squamous (keratinizing), mucinous ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandspleomorphicadenoma.html))
  - Tyrosine crystals and intravascular tumor deposits may occur (do not indicate malignancy)
- Capsule:  
  - Major glands: thick, well defined  
  - Minor glands: circumscribed, often lacking a true capsule; can extend into fat while remaining benign ([Hn Atlas, p.978](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/HN_Atlas.pdf#page=978))
- Cytologic features: bland, lacks significant atypia, mitoses, or necrosis
- Malignant transformation: invasion, marked pleomorphism, necrosis, perineural/vascular invasion  

![Triphasic architecture—epithelial, myoepithelial, stroma](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/imgau/salivaryglandspleomorphicadenomaxu08new.jpg)
![Myxoid, chondroid, and epithelial elements](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-public-figures-830130787988/textbook_figures_web_v1/hn_atlas/hn_atlas_p0979_fig01_fig_20_6.jpeg)

## Cytology

- Cellularity: variable  
- Features:
  - Mixture of myoepithelial cells (plasmacytoid, spindle, oval/round) and ductal epithelial cells  
  - Fibrillar magenta stroma (Romanowsky stain; gray-green chondromyxoid on Papanicolaou)  
  - Cell clusters: cohesive, bland cytology, round-oval nuclei, fine chromatin  
  - Background: bluish-purple mucoid/fibromyxoid stroma  
- Key point: diagnosis of PA requires finding triphasic architectural features; other benign salivary neoplasms may yield similar cytologies—Milan system diagnosis of “benign neoplasm” has <5% risk of malignancy, but is not exclusive to PA ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandsneoplasmbenign.html))  
![Fibrillary stroma with bland basaloid epithelial cells](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/imgau/salivaryglandspleomorphicadenomabychkov01new.jpg)

## Ancillary Tests

- **Immunohistochemistry:**  
  - Ductal (epithelial) cells: cytokeratins (AE1/AE3, CK7, CAM 5.2), vimentin  
  - Myoepithelial cells: GFAP, S100, SOX10, α-smooth muscle actin, calponin, p40, p63  
  - PLAG1 and HMGA2: nuclear positivity by IHC corresponds to gene fusions if present (surrogate markers) ([Hn Atlas, p.979](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/source_pdfs/HN_Atlas.pdf#page=979))
- **Molecular:**  
  - PLAG1 or HMGA2 gene rearrangements in ~70% of PAs, often mutually exclusive, sometimes overlap ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandspleomorphicadenoma.html))
- **Negative stains:**  
  - Melanocytic markers (MelanA, HMB45) are negative
- **EM**: may confirm myoepithelial differentiation if needed  

## Radiology

- MRI: well defined or bosselated border, typically hyperintense on T2-weighted images ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandspleomorphicadenoma.html))  
- Lobulated margins, pseudopodic extensions possible  

## Differential Diagnosis

- **Carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma**  
  - Shows frank malignancy: marked nuclear pleomorphism, necrosis, invasion, perineural/vascular involvement  
  - Both may contain PLAG1 or HMGA2 fusions; use morphologic criteria for carcinoma ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandspleomorphicadenoma.html))  
- **Myoepithelioma and myoepithelial carcinoma**  
  - Composed almost exclusively of myoepithelial cells (plasmacytoid/spindle/epithelioid); lacks triphasic/ductal elements; monomorphic histology ([WHO](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/WHO/WHO_HTML/HN/Salivary_Gland_Myoepithelioma.html))
- **Basal cell adenoma**  
  - Biphasic basaloid morphology, peripheral palisading, little to no myxoid stroma, absent true triphasic pattern ([WHO](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/WHO/WHO_HTML/HN/Basal_Cell_Adenoma.html))
- **Polymorphous adenocarcinoma**  
  - Variable architectural and cytologic features but lacks true triphasic/PA pattern (distinction rests on finding classic ductal, myoepithelial, and stromal elements) ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandspleomorphicadenoma.html))
- **Adenoid cystic carcinoma**  
  - May have cribriform/tubular areas, small basaloid cells with infiltrative growth, perineural invasion is frequent, and lacks classic PA triphasic pattern ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandsadenoidcystic.html))
- **Epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma**  
  - Dual populations of ductal and clear myoepithelial cells, prominent infiltrative edges; lacks triphasic stromal features  
- **Squamous cell carcinoma**  
  - Can show squamous metaplasia/keratinization like PA, but lacks triphasic diagnostic features of PA  
- **Canalicular adenoma**  
  - Monomorphic, canal-like cords in a vascular stroma, little to no myxoid matrix, no basal/myoepithelial layer, almost always minor gland (esp. upper lip) ([WHO](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/WHO/WHO_HTML/HN/Canalicular_Adenoma.html), [Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandscanalicularadenoma.html))
- **Cystadenoma**  
  - Unilocular/multicystic lesion, papillary architecture common, oncocytic cells may predominate, no triphasic features, minimal stroma ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandscystadenoma.html))
- **Sclerosing polycystic adenoma**  
  - Well-delineated, small nodules with irregular bilayered ducts/acini in sclerotic stroma, apocrine/ductal changes, resembles breast fibrocystic change, cohesive IHC pattern, lacks PA triphasia ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandssclerosingpolycysticadenoma.html))
- **Lymphadenoma / Sebaceous lymphadenoma**  
  - Nests/islands of bland epithelium (often sebaceous) in lymphoid stroma, lacks typical triphasic PA pattern ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandssebaceousadenoma.html))
- **Adenomatoid hyperplasia / Sialadenosis**  
  - Non-neoplastic; lobular hyperplasia or hypertrophy of normal salivary tissue, lacks encapsulation/architectural diversity seen in PA ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandsadenomatoidhyperplasia.html))
- **Nodular oncocytic hyperplasia**  
  - Multifocal clusters of oncocytes, frequently bilateral; lacks encapsulation, lacks ductal/myoepithelial biphasia, not a neoplasm ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandsoncocytosis.html))
- **Oncocytoma**  
  - Well-circumscribed epithelial neoplasm formed by sheets/nests of oncocytes, no myxoid or chondroid stroma, not triphasic ([WHO](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/WHO/WHO_HTML/CYTO_LUNG/Benign_Salivary_Gland_Neoplasms_Of_The_Respiratory_Tract_Include_Pleomorphic_Adenoma_Myoepithelioma_And_Oncocytoma_And_Closely_Resemble_Their_Salivary_Gland_Counterparts.html), [Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandsoncocytosis.html))

## Prognostic Factors

- Recurrence risk: 15–25% with enucleation; much lower with complete excision; typically within 18 months but can occur up to 50 years later ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandspleomorphicadenoma.html))
- Recurrence risk is higher with incomplete excision, parotid location (due to pseudopodic growth), or capsule rupture  
- Malignant transformation rate ~5%, especially with:
  - Multiple recurrences
  - Submandibular site
  - Older age
  - Larger tumor size
  - Prominent hyalinization
  - Increased mitotic activity
  - Prior radiation exposure ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandspleomorphicadenoma.html))
- **Benign metastasizing mixed tumors:** rare entity; may develop after excision, can appear years/decades later as metastatic PA in distant sites, retaining benign morphology ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandspleomorphicadenoma.html))

## Illustrative Cases

- Cases described in literature: 6-year-old girl with parotid PA; 28-year-old man with submandibular mass; 54-year-old man with upper lip swelling for 10 years; 84-year-old man with parotid lesion ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/salivaryglandspleomorphicadenoma.html))
- Recurrent PA: multiple nodules (“shotgun pellet” pattern), parotid predilection after prior excision  
- Metastasizing PA associated with recurrent PLAG1/HMGA2 fusion events

cards.title: Salivary gland myoepithelioma
cards.excerpt: Entity: Salivary gland myoepithelioma Section: differential_diagnosis The well-defined borders of the tumour and the lack of invasive growth distinguish ME from myoepithelial carcinoma. The characteristic basaloid biphasic pattern, peripheral palisading, and minimal to absent myxoid stroma of basal cell adenoma help to separate it from ME. Monomorphic histology and rare or absent ductal structures in ME separate it from pleomorphic adenoma. Distinguishing from soft tissue ME may be difficult, given the overlapping histological features and the presence of PLAG1 gene rearrangements in both.

cards.title: Pleomorphic adenoma — Benign tumor: surgical resection with negative margin is considered curative
cards.excerpt:
Enucleation is associated with 15 - 25% risk of local recurrence
Recurrences are usually within 18 months but can be up to 50 years later (Arch Pathol Lab Med 2008;132:1445)
Risk of malignant transformation is ~5%
Risk factors for malignant transformation: multiple recurrences, submandibular location, older age, larger size, prominent hyalinization, increased mitotic rate (if present, sample tumor more thoroughly), radiation exposure

cards.title: Pleomorphic adenoma — Typically has 3 components
cards.excerpt:
Epithelial (ductal) component forming the inner layer of cysts and tubules
Myoepithelial cells as the outer layer of cysts and tubules and scattered within the myxoid stroma
Cytology of myoepithelial cells can be plasmacytoid, spindled, epithelioid, clear or stellate shaped

cards.title: Pleomorphic adenoma — Stromal component is typically myxoid, chondroid or myxochondroid
cards.excerpt:
It can also be hyalinized or fibrotic
Metaplastic changes may be seen, e.g. adipose metaplasia, osseous metaplasia, squamous metaplasia (sometimes with keratinization), sebaceous metaplasia and mucinous metaplasia
Intravascular permeation has been reported in a small percentage of cases and does not increase the risk of recurrence or distant metastasis
It is proposed to be a phenomenon associated with surgical manipulation (Am J Surg Pathol 2012;36:1674)

cards.title: Pleomorphic adenoma — Typical feature is its unique fibrillary stroma
cards.excerpt:
Mixture of myoepithelial cells, ductal cells and extracellular stroma
Myoepithelial cells are usually the predominant cell type with various cytomorphology, including round, polygonal, plasmacytoid, spindle, etc.
Ductal cells show bland cytologic features with organized honeycombing or ductal arrangement
Extracellular matrix shows characteristic feathery / fibrillary borders and bright magenta color on Romanowsky type stain and gray-green chondromyxoid features on Papanicolaou stain

cards.title: Pleomorphic adenoma — Essential features
cards.heading: Essential features
cards.text_excerpt:
Primary pulmonary pleomorphic adenoma is a very rare benign tumor that tends to arise in the large airways
Tumors tend to show small, branching, double layered ductules rather than ducts and less cartilaginous stroma as compared to pleomorphic adenomas arising in the salivary gland
Keratin and vimentin staining of the epithelial component supports diagnosis of primary pulmonary tumor as opposed to only keratin staining in salivary gland tumors (Arch Pathol Lab Med 2003;127:621)
Prognosis is generally good, but cases of carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenom have been reported

Explicit inclusion: 'Benign metastasizing mixed tumors' as a rare event, should be in Prognostic Factors section

In the Ancillary Tests section, under molecular, it should be noted that both PLAG1 and HMGA2 gene rearrangements are seen in PA "often mutually exclusive; sometimes overlapping" (subtlety from Pathology Outlines)

In Prognostic Factors, explicitly state the time course for recurrence: recurrences can occur up to 50 years later (from Pathology Outlines) and are usually within 18 months, both are relevant for education

Under Clinical Issues/Prognosis: 'Risk of malignant transformation is increased with multiple recurrences, submandibular location, older age, larger size, prominent hyalinization, increased mitotic rate, radiation exposure' (Pathology Outlines); draft only half covers this list
redundant: "PLAG1 and/or HMGA2 gene rearrangements present in ~70% of cases" (Key Facts) and essentially restated in Essential and Desirable Diagnostic Criteria, Etiology/Pathogenesis, and Ancillary Tests. Consolidate or clarify different contexts.

"Recurrence risk increased with incomplete excision (esp. in parotid due to pseudopods); malignant transformation risk ~5%" (Key Facts) recapitulates later content almost verbatim in Prognostic Factors and Clinical Issues.
confusing: "PLAG1 and/or HMGA2 IHC positivity"—not clear in context if this is a desirable diagnostic feature or a surrogate, and what 'positivity' refers to for the user; should be more explicit: 'nuclear positivity by IHC for the corresponding fusion gene.'
"Milan system: diagnostic for a benign neoplasm with <5% risk of malignancy" is not well situated or referenced and should be integrated or clarified in context (currently abrupt and ambiguous).
entity_conflation: Mentions of 'rarely congenital (hamartomatous variant in infants, indistinct from typical PA)'—this refers to salivary gland anlage tumor (SGAT), which is not considered a true PA in modern WHO classification; should clarify and distinguish.

In differential, inclusion of 'adenoid cystic carcinoma, polymorphous adenocarcinoma, epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma' without sufficient separation of which features distinguish each individually from PA as demanded by Pathology Outlines/WHO definitions.
off_organ_or_offtopic: Mentions in Cytology and Macroscopic sections referencing Milan System 'diagnostic for a benign salivary gland neoplasm' do not clarify that this entity is specifically PA as opposed to other benign processes; could mislead if not clarified.
